A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of circulating tumour or cancer cells in the peripheral blood is not uncommon and may be a source of confusion for the pathologist.
the presence of carcinocythema in the circulation of patients with primary lung cancer is rare and is not necessarily associated with the presence of bone marrow metastases.
the buffy-coats of patients with metastatic oat-cell cancer of the lung may show carcinoma cells in the buffy-coated preparation, and that these carcinoma cells may be confused with myeloblasts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diagnosis of carcinocythema should not be based solely on morphologic features.
the presence of cancer cells in the peripheral blood is an indication of the presence of cancer elsewhere in the body.
the presence of circulating tumour cell clusters in the blood is a potential marker of disease progression.
